title: GuardDuty: an access key is being used from an unknown country
intro: GuardDuty raised a HIGH finding at 03:12: API calls from an IP in a country where you have no staff, using the access key of the IAM user 'ci-deployer'. That key was committed to a public GitHub repo two hours ago by accident. Every minute counts: crypto-mining bots scan GitHub for AWS keys within minutes.

steps.prompt: Contain first: deactivate the key AKIAEXAMPLELEAKED01 belonging to ci-deployer (deactivate, don't delete yet, so the evidence is kept).
expected_commands: aws iam update-access-key --user-name ci-deployer --access-key-id AKIAEXAMPLELEAKED01 --status Inactive
steps.fake_output: (no output: the key is now inactive and all calls with it fail)
steps.hint: update-access-key --status Inactive is instant and reversible.

steps.prompt: Deactivating the key doesn't kill temporary credentials the attacker may already have created from it. Check what the attacker did: look up CloudTrail events made with access key AKIAEXAMPLELEAKED01.
steps.fake_output:
EventTime             EventName              SourceIP        Region
2026-09-28T03:05:41Z  GetCallerIdentity      185.220.101.4   us-east-1
2026-09-28T03:06:02Z  CreateUser             185.220.101.4   us-east-1   (userName=support-backup)
2026-09-28T03:06:05Z  CreateAccessKey        185.220.101.4   us-east-1   (userName=support-backup)
2026-09-28T03:07:30Z  RunInstances           185.220.101.4   ap-southeast-1  (count=20, type=c5.4xlarge)

steps.prompt: The attacker created a backdoor user 'support-backup' with its own key. Find that user's access keys.
Deactivate the backdoor key AKIAEXAMPLEBACKDOOR9 of support-backup.
expected_commands: aws iam update-access-key --user-name support-backup --access-key-id AKIAEXAMPLEBACKDOOR9 --status Inactive
steps.fake_output: (no output: the backdoor key is inactive)
steps.hint: Same command as the first step, for the other user and key.

steps.prompt: The attacker launched 20 instances in ap-southeast-1, a region you don't use, for crypto-mining. List the running instances there.
steps.fake_output:
InstanceId            Type         LaunchTime            KeyName
i-0f1e2d3c4b5a60001   c5.4xlarge   2026-09-28T03:07:31Z  (none)
i-0f1e2d3c4b5a60002   c5.4xlarge   2026-09-28T03:07:31Z  (none)
... (20 instances)
steps.hint: Attackers pick regions you don't watch, so always pass --region.

resolution: The order of operations is the lesson. First contain the leaked key (deactivate, don't delete, so its history stays attributable). Then assume the attacker established persistence: here, a new IAM user with its own key, which would have survived rotating the original key. Then clean up the damage: 20 mining instances in a region nobody watched, costing thousands of dollars a day. Next steps not shown: terminate those instances after snapshotting one for forensics; delete the backdoor user; revoke any role sessions the attacker created (an inline policy denying sessions issued before now); check every region, not just the one GuardDuty named; and open a case with AWS Support, who often waive fraudulent charges. Root causes: a long-lived access key existed for CI at all (GitHub Actions should use OIDC federation to assume a role, see cicd-tutorial-005), and no pre-commit secret scanning (gitleaks) caught it. An SCP limiting usable regions would have blocked the mining launch entirely.
